questions.problem:
Suppose that the function $f(x,y)$ and all of its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U.$ Which of the following pairs could represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y)?$

I. ${f}_{x}(x,y)=x+4y$ and ${f}_{y}(x,y)=3x-y$

II. ${f}_{x}(x,y)=2x$ and ${f}_{y}(x,y)=0$

III. ${f}_{x}(x,y)=2x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y$ and ${f}_{y}(x,y)={e}^{y}-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y$
questions.worked_solution:
Since the function and its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ the mixed partial derivatives must be equal, that is, ${f}_{xy}(x,y)={f}_{yx}(x,y).$ Let's check if this condition is true for each of our pairs of first-order partial derivatives.

- For the first pair, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x+4y)=4 \\ {f}_{yx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(3x-y)=3.\end{aligned}
$$

As ${f}_{xy}(x,y)\ne {f}_{yx}(x,y)$, the first pair cannot represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y).$

- For the second pair, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2x)=0 \\ {f}_{yx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(0)=0.\end{aligned}
$$

As ${f}_{xy}(x,y)={f}_{yx}(x,y)$, the second pair could represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y).$

- For the third pair, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y) \\  & =0+\operatorname{cos}⁡x\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡y) \\  & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y, \\ {f}_{yx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{y}-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y) \\  & =0-\operatorname{sin}⁡y\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡x \\  & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y.\end{aligned}
$$

As ${f}_{xy}(x,y)={f}_{yx}(x,y)$,  the third pair could represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y).$

Therefore, the correct answer is 'II and III only'.

questions.problem: Given that the function $f(x,y)$ and all of its higher-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ evaluate ${f}_{yxx}(1,1)$ if ${f}_{xy}(x,y)=y{e}^{xy}(2+xy).$
questions.worked_solution:
As the higher-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ the mixed partial derivatives must be equal. Hence, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{yxx}(x,y) & ={f}_{xyx}(x,y) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({f}_{xy}(x,y)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(y{e}^{xy}(2+xy)) \\  & ={y}^{2}{e}^{xy}(2+xy)+{y}^{2}{e}^{xy} \\  & ={y}^{2}{e}^{xy}(3+xy).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(1,1):$

$$
{f}_{yxx}(1,1)=(1)^{2}{e}^{1\cdot 1}(3+(1)(1))=4e\,\,
$$

questions.problem:
Suppose that the function $f(x,y)$ and all of its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U.$ Which of the following pairs could represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y)?$

I. ${f}_{x}(x,y)={x}^{2}-2y$ and ${f}_{y}(x,y)={y}^{2}-2x$

II. ${f}_{x}(x,y)=\sqrt{\frac{y}{x}}+3{x}^{2}y$ and ${f}_{y}(x,y)=\sqrt{\frac{x}{y}}+{x}^{3}$

III. ${f}_{x}(x,y)={e}^{x+1}\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-1)$ and ${f}_{y}(x,y)={e}^{\sqrt{y}}$
questions.worked_solution:
Since the function and its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ the mixed partial derivatives must be equal, that is, ${f}_{xy}(x,y)={f}_{yx}(x,y).$ Let's check if this condition is true for each of our pairs of first-order partial derivatives.

- For the first pair, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-2y)=-2 \\ {f}_{yx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{2}-2x)=-2.\end{aligned}
$$

As ${f}_{xy}(x,y)={f}_{yx}(x,y)$, the first pair could represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y).$

- For the second pair, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\sqrt{\frac{y}{x}}+3{x}^{2}y)=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{yx}}+3{x}^{2} \\ {f}_{yx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\sqrt{\frac{x}{y}}+{x}^{3})=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{xy}}+3{x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

As ${f}_{xy}(x,y)={f}_{yx}(x,y)$, the second pair could represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y).$

- For the third pair, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{x+1}\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-1))=0 \\ {f}_{yx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{\sqrt{y}})=0.\end{aligned}
$$

As ${f}_{xy}(x,y)={f}_{yx}(x,y)$,  the third pair could represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y).$

Therefore, the correct answer is 'I, II and III'.

questions.problem: Given that the function $f(x,y)$ and all of its higher-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ evaluate ${f}_{yxy}(1,2)$ if ${f}_{yy}(x,y)={x}^{2}{y}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x-y).$
questions.worked_solution:
As the higher-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ the mixed partial derivatives must be equal. Hence, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{yxy}(x,y) & ={f}_{yyx}(x,y) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({f}_{yy}(x,y)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}{y}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x-y)) \\  & ={y}^{3}(2x\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(2x-y)+{x}^{2}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(2x-y)\cdot 2) \\  & =2x{y}^{3}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x-y)+x\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x-y)).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(1,2):$

$$
{f}_{xyx}(1,2)=2\cdot 1\cdot {2}^{3}\cdot (\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot 1-2)+1\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(2\cdot 1-2))=16.
$$

questions.problem:
Suppose that a function $f(x,y,z)$ and all of its higher-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ and that

$$
\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}=\frac{x{e}^{yz}}{x+y},\,\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂z}=-\frac{z{e}^{yz}}{x+y}.
$$

 

Evaluate the following expression at the point $(1,1,0):$

$$
\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂y∂x∂y}+\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂z∂x∂z}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
As the higher-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ the mixed partial derivatives must be equal. 

Hence, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂y∂x∂y} & =\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂x∂{y}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{x{e}^{yz}}{x+y}) \\  & ={e}^{yz}\cdot (\frac{1\cdot (x+y)-x\cdot 1}{(x+y)^{2}}) \\  & =\frac{y{e}^{yz}}{(x+y)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

In addition, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂z∂x∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂z}) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(-\frac{z{e}^{yz}}{x+y}) \\  & =-\frac{1}{x+y}\cdot ({e}^{yz}+yz{e}^{yz}) \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{yz}(1+yz)}{x+y}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we evaluate both partial derivatives at the point $(1,1,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂x∂y∂x}{|}_{(1,1,0)} & =\frac{1\cdot {e}^{1\cdot 0}}{(1+1)^{2}}=\frac{1}{4} \\ \frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂z∂x∂z}{|}_{(1,1,0)} & =-\frac{{e}^{1\cdot 0}(1+1\cdot 0)}{1+1}=-\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂x∂y∂x}{|}_{(1,1,0)}+\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂z∂x∂z}{|}_{(1,1,0)} & =\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{2}=-\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$
